I just saw Rubio trying to diss other Republicans (I'm assuming Cruz or Paul) as "hiding" VATs in their tax codes, and saying conservatives wouldn't want that.

Why is this a thing? I consider myself to be fairly conservative, and I've always liked the idea of a VAT for government revenue over income tax because it ends up acting more as a consumption tax than a tax on your success. Consumption taxes are the ones that hit the super reach (read as: inheritance families) that don't have income or produce anymore, and they reward individual responsibility.

Was Rubio just saying any tax is bad, or is there some reason that Conservatives wouldn't want a VAT?
Can someone walk me through why a conservative would be against the thought of a VAT?

I'm in the same boat as you. I think a flat tax on all goods and services sold is a great idea. I'd make it around 5-7%. Certainly no more that 10% (really you don't want state and local combined to get over 10%).

People will complain "that's not enough". 5% of the total US output is plenty of money to run it. Shit, you could probably get by with 1%.

People will complain "it's not fair to poorer people". Bullshit. Everyone pays the same rate, no need to discriminate.

People will have other nonsense complaints - I don't think there is a valid argument against a flat tax on all goods and services - including stocks and other crazy shit Wall St. sells. Capital gains tax would be gone - you paid a tax when you initially bought the investment and the person you sell it to will pay a tax on any increase in value it may undergo. You don't get writeoffs if it loses money - please do try to select better investments. And yes, you will be charged for every "trade" - your crazy ass investment strategies are a hazard that must be hedged against.

I'd like to see more "opt-in" government. That is, you only pay for the goods / services you're interested in. That way, if some bullshit legislation gets passed, like the healthcare nonsense, you can choose whether or not it affects you. For something more complicated, like paying for public schooling, it would require more thought. Something like "you are educated for free as a child, should you have children, you must opt in to pay for their educations".

It would be nice for something like roads so that when some small group of activist cyclists want to create bike lanes or otherwise disrupt normal traffic, it means they will pay for it by themselves and, conversely, people who own cars won't have to tolerate bicycles on the main streets.

My biggest problem with it is that it's completely hidden. At least with a straight up sales tax you know you're being taxed. With a VAT tax, the price of everything goes up, consumption goes down, the economy is damaged - and the consumer never realizes that the reason everything is so expensive is because of a tax hidden inside the manufacturing process. And politicians love this. It's very much like the way governments "tax" by inflating the money supply. They love it because anybody not paying attention doesn't realize it's happening - and that's 90% of voters.

Then there's the difficulty of keeping track of it - the huge administrative costs of managing a tax at every. single. level. of the manufacturing process. Think about how many steps and different manufactured items have to be brought together to make a car. A pencil, even.

To me it just sounds like an underhanded and inefficient way to raise tax revenue.

The argument against it is that it was used in Europe to rapidly grow the welfare state. The Laffer curve puts limits on the amount of money you can collect from income taxes. You don't have that problem with a consumption tax like the VAT. Even small increases in the tax will take a lot of money out of the economy but, because it taxes many transactions, it's difficult to see the damage it does to the economy. Business slows and living standards decrease but the people don't have something simple like a pay stub to look at to understand how it's happening.

The candidates supporting a VAT propose eliminating other taxes at the same time. Opponents argue that the democrats will keep the VAT and bring the old taxes back when they get in power again.
